prior_scan_disposition.note: This scan covers 4 blog posts newly entering the content-quality-loop. All 4 files changed from 'unreviewed' to 'ai-reviewed' in reviewStatus. The adjudication post also gained a developer lens framing. Body content remains unchanged — this represents a first full-content scan of these posts.

findings.description: 'Most agent frameworks handle this with vibes' — quantitative claim ('most') without evidence or citation. Characterizes an entire class of systems without naming examples or citing comparative analysis.
findings.suggestion: Replace with a scoped claim: 'Many agent frameworks lack structured consequence tracing' or name specific frameworks for comparison. Alternatively, hedge: 'In our survey of N frameworks, none included...'
findings.context: Most agent frameworks handle this with vibes. The model picks whatever seems reasonable, ships it, and you discover the knock-on effects when something breaks downstream.

findings.description: State Department reporting cost estimate ($1-3 million per cycle) attributed to 'comparable State Department reporting exercises' without a specific citation. The Sources section includes no State Department cost reference. This figure drives the Layer 1 conclusion.
findings.suggestion: Either cite the specific comparable (e.g., ICCPR reporting cost data from a GAO or State Department budget document) or hedge explicitly: 'We estimate, based on the scale of ICCPR periodic review exercises, that ICESCR reporting would cost...' and flag the estimate as the authors' inference rather than documented fact.
findings.context: The reporting cycle for the U.S. under the ICCPR has run at roughly $1–3 million per cycle in staff time and contractor costs, based on comparable State Department reporting exercises.

findings.description: 'Research suggests that the majority of organizations lack adequate auditability for AI agent decisions (McKinsey, 2025)' — the parenthetical citation lacks a specific report title, making verification difficult. McKinsey publishes dozens of AI reports annually.
findings.suggestion: Expand the citation to include the specific report title: 'Research suggests... (McKinsey, "[Report Title]", 2025).' If the specific source cannot be identified, replace with a more verifiable claim or drop the parenthetical.
findings.context: Research suggests that the majority of organizations lack adequate auditability for AI agent decisions (McKinsey, 2025).

findings.description: E-prime violation: 'There's a better way.' ('There's' expands to 'There is'). The project glossary header states 'All definitions follow E-prime.' Blog posts should maintain the same standard.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'A better approach exists.' or 'We found a better way.'
findings.context: There's a better way. It comes from a 1971 psychometrics textbook.

findings.description: E-prime violation: 'Gf is what you need when you haven't seen the problem before.' Two forms of 'to be' in one sentence.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'Gf — the capacity you draw on when you encounter a problem for the first time.'
findings.context: Gf is what you need when you haven't seen the problem before.

findings.description: E-prime violation: 'The question wasn't *what* to build — the architecture was set. The question was *how to sequence*...' — three forms of 'to be' in two sentences.
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'The architecture had already settled *what* to build. The open question: *how to sequence the implementation*.'
findings.context: The question wasn't *what* to build — the architecture was set. The question was *how to sequence the implementation*. Three options emerged:

findings.description: E-prime violation: 'The analogy isn't perfect.' ('isn't' = 'is not').
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'The analogy stretches at certain points.' or 'The analogy carries transfer risks.'
findings.context: The analogy isn't perfect. Biological neural circuits operate in continuous time with real sensory feedback.

findings.description: E-prime violation: 'The result is an architecture with principled grounding...' ('is').
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'The result: an architecture with principled grounding...' (colon substitution) or 'This work produced an architecture with principled grounding...'
findings.context: The result is an architecture with principled grounding, documented limitations, and a maturation pathway that mirrors how humans actually learn

findings.description: 'INCOSE emergence theory' — INCOSE (International Council on Systems Engineering) acronym used without expansion on first use. Also appears unexpanded in pattern-generators.md line 73. The unratified glossary does not include this term.
findings.suggestion: Expand on first use: 'INCOSE (International Council on Systems Engineering) emergence theory' — or add INCOSE to the glossary with a definition. The pattern-generators post can then reference the glossary entry.
findings.context: combining INCOSE emergence theory with Popperian falsificationism at the final tier

findings.description: E-prime violation: 'The `auto_generated: true` flag is visible to receiving agents.' ('is visible').
findings.suggestion: Rewrite: 'The `auto_generated: true` flag appears visible to receiving agents.' or 'Receiving agents can see the `auto_generated: true` flag.'
findings.context: The `auto_generated: true` flag is visible to receiving agents.

epistemic_flags: First scan of these 4 blog posts — no convergence data available. Prior scans targeted different files (src/pages/action/, src/content/).
E-prime violations dominate findings (6/10). The unratified glossary.ts header declares E-prime compliance; blog post body text has not yet received systematic E-prime review.

The ratification-cost post (how-much-would-ratification-cost.md) showed notably strong fair-witness practice overall — the uncited State Dept figure represents an exception in an otherwise well-sourced document.
The pattern-generators post explicitly flags circular evaluation risk and analogical transfer risk — strong epistemic self-disclosure that reduces the weight of the fair-witness finding.
